211.title: The Chinese and Greek painters
211.hook: one team paints a wall, the other only polishes theirs until it mirrors everything (Masnavi 1.3467ff)
211.tomorrow: of course there are rude people
211.howItsDone: Sufi teachers speak of polishing the heart, and some describe dhikr, the remembrance of God, as the polish that clears it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the three fish, and the one that left before the net came. Leave in time.

Some people fill a room. They've got the stories, the opinions, the funny voices, and they're great company. And then there's the other kind: the friend you tell something to, and somehow, when they listen, you see your own life more clearly. They don't add much. They reflect. You leave feeling more like yourself. Both are gifts. But Rumi tells a story about a contest between the two, a painting contest judged by a king. One team brings a hundred colors. The other brings none at all.
screen: `SOME PEOPLE FILL A ROOM.` → `SOME PEOPLE REFLECT.` → `THE CHINESE AND GREEK PAINTERS.`

segments.voice: It's in Book One of the Masnavi. The Chinese painters say: we're the better artists. The Greeks, by which Rumi means the painters of the Byzantine lands, say: no, we are. So the king sets a test. Each team gets a room, facing each other, with a curtain hung between. The Chinese ask the king for a hundred colors, and every morning they collect more paint from his treasury. The Greeks say: no colors are right for our work. All we do is remove the rust. They shut their door and polish, day after day, until the wall is as clear and bright as the sky. The Chinese finish first, and beat drums for joy. The king comes in and is amazed by their painting. Then he goes to the Greeks, and they pull back the curtain. All the Chinese pictures, reflected in that polished wall, shine back even more beautifully than on the wall where they were painted. Rumi tells us who the Greeks are: the Sufis, he says, who don't rely on study and books and learning, but have polished their hearts clean of greed, envy and malice. A heart polished like that is a mirror. It can receive every image, without end. Rumi isn't saying here that learning is useless. He's saying the heart's work isn't adding more, it's clearing away, and a clear heart takes in the whole world. Your line: polish the mirror.
screen: `A CONTEST BEFORE THE KING.` · `A HUNDRED COLORS, OR NONE.` · `THE POLISHED WALL SHINES BRIGHTER.` · then, large: `POLISH THE MIRROR.`

segments.voice: Picture a mirror inside you, a little dusty from the week. With each out-breath, imagine one layer of dust coming off: a worry, a grudge, an old comparison. Don't add anything; just clear, slowly, the way you'd clean a window or a table.
Mirror. One team paints with a hundred colors; the other only polishes its wall, until it reflects everything more beautifully, like a heart cleared of greed and envy. Today's word.
Your line: polish the mirror. A clear heart takes in everything. Until tomorrow.

212.title: Of course there are rude people
212.hook: when offended, ask: could the world exist without shameless people? (Meditations 9.42)
212.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus often use this passage, and the similar morning reflection in Book Two, to prepare for difficult people before the day begins, so that rudeness brings less shock and more patience.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Chinese and Greek painters, and the wall polished into a mirror. Polish the mirror.

Somebody cuts you off in traffic, and you hear yourself say it: unbelievable. A man talks through the whole movie. Unbelievable. A coworker takes credit for your idea in the meeting. Unbelievable! But is it? Honestly, it's about the most believable thing in the world. It happens every day, everywhere, and has for as long as there have been people. Part of what stings isn't the rudeness. It's the surprise, as if the world had broken a promise. Marcus, who dealt with a great many difficult people, had a cure for the surprise.
screen: `UNBELIEVABLE.` → `THE MOST BELIEVABLE THING IN THE WORLD.` → `OF COURSE THERE ARE RUDE PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Book Nine, section forty-two. When you're offended by someone's shameless behavior, Marcus writes, ask yourself right away, in George Long's words: "Is it possible, then, that shameless men should not be in the world? It is not possible." So don't ask for the impossible. This person is simply one of the ones who have to exist. Say the same, he adds, about the dishonest person and the one who lets you down. The moment you remember that such people must be in the world, you'll be kinder to each one. Marcus isn't excusing rudeness. He's taking away the shock, so you can respond instead of react. Then a practical question: what quality has nature given you to meet this? Against the unkind person, he says, gentleness, like an antidote. And one more turn, a bit uncomfortable: if someone let you down, ask whether the fault is partly yours for expecting what they were never going to give. This is the same man who started his mornings telling himself: today I'll meet the meddling, the ungrateful, the arrogant. Not to be gloomy. To be ready. It closes our cooked week well. Dig within for the good. Let the heat soften you. The story on top, not the thing itself. Put the bitter cucumber down. Leave in time. Polish the mirror. And when the rude person arrives, as they will: of course. Your line.

segments.voice: Picture a moment where someone might be rude: the commute, a meeting, a phone call, the checkout line. Let it happen in your mind, feel the old flash of surprise, and say inside: of course. Then picture yourself meeting it with a little gentleness.
Antidote. Marcus's word for gentleness, met against someone's rudeness, so you respond instead of react. Today's word.
Your line: of course. That closes a whole week of being cooked. Rest well.

213.title: Who is at the door?
213.hook: a lover knocks, says "it is I," and is sent away until he learns to answer "it is you" (Masnavi 1.3056ff)
213.howItsDone: In Sufi teaching, this story is often told to describe the lessening of the ego on the way to God, and many readers also take it as a picture of selfless love between people.

segments.voice: Last week closed with Marcus: of course there are rude people. Your line was of course.

You knock on a door, and from inside someone calls: who is it? And you say, without thinking: it's me. As if me were the most obvious thing in the world. Couples do it on the phone. Kids do it at the front door. Me! We say it all day long: my plan, my turn, my way, my feelings about it. A new week starts today. It's called guests, and it's about who we let in. And it begins at a door, with a very short story of Rumi's.
screen: `WHO IS IT? IT'S ME.` → `A WEEK OF GUESTS.` → `WHO IS AT THE DOOR?`

segments.voice: It's in Book One of the Masnavi. A man comes to the door of the one he loves and knocks. From inside, the beloved asks: who are you? He answers: it's I. And the beloved says: go away. This isn't the time. There's no place at a table like this for someone raw. Remember raw from the chickpea? Not yet cooked, still hard, still full of himself. So the man goes away. For a whole year he travels, burning with the pain of separation, and in Rumi's words, the fire cooks him. Then he comes back. He paces around the house, afraid some careless word will slip out again. He knocks. The voice inside asks: who is at the door? This time he says: it is you. You, who hold my heart. And the beloved says: since you are I, come in. There isn't room in this house for two I's. The story works on a few levels. On the surface, it's about love between people: real love has less me in it. But Rumi is talking about God. The seeker comes to the door full of himself, and the door stays shut. Only when the self has been cooked down, when he can say it is you, is there room. Sufi teachers put it this way: it isn't that he disappears. It's that his I no longer stands between. That's a long road. But there's a small version of it at any kitchen table: arriving with it's me, or arriving with it's you. Your line: it is you.
screen: `WHO ARE YOU? IT'S I.` · `A YEAR OF BURNING.` · `IT IS YOU. COME IN.` · then, large: `NO ROOM FOR TWO I'S.`

segments.voice: Notice how often I or me shows up in your thoughts, even now: I'm doing this right, I'm tired, me, me. Each time, let it soften and pass like footsteps going by a door, and rest in what's here without the name tag. If you pray, you can rest in God's presence without saying who you are.
Beloved. A lover says it's I and is turned away, then returns after a year and says it's you, and the beloved lets him in. Today's word.
Your line: it is you. Less me, and more room. Day two hundred thirteen.

214.title: The guest house
214.hook: a new arrival each morning, joy or grief or meanness, and each to be welcomed (Masnavi 5.3644ff)
214.howItsDone: Readers of Rumi, and some meditation teachers, use this picture of moods as guests, naming what arrives and letting it stay and leave, rather than taking it as who they are.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the lover at the door learned to answer: it is you. No room for two I's.

You wake up, and before your feet touch the floor, something's already there. A heaviness, for no reason. Or a buzzy excitement. Or a low irritation that'll follow you to the coffee machine. You didn't invite it. It just arrived in the night. It's easy to treat these moods as who we are. I'm anxious. I'm a grump today. As if the mood owned the house. Rumi had another way to see it, in a passage a modern poem was later built on. Today, back to what Rumi himself wrote.
screen: `SOMETHING ARRIVES IN THE NIGHT.` → `AS IF THE MOOD OWNED THE HOUSE.` → `THE GUEST HOUSE.`

segments.voice: It's in Book Five of the Masnavi. Every day, Rumi says, at every moment, a different thought comes into your heart like an honored guest. Treat each thought as a person, he says, because a person's worth comes from their thoughts and their soul. Then the surprising part. If a sad thought arrives and seems to be chasing away your joy, it may be making room for joy. It sweeps the house clear, he says, so that new joy, from the source of all good, can come in. It shakes the yellow leaves off the branch of the heart, so fresh green leaves can grow. It pulls up the old roots of happiness, so new ones can come from beyond. So be welcoming, Rumi says, even to the sorrow. Don't slam the door. You don't know what it's bringing. That modern poem opens by calling a human being a guest house. It's a modern rendering, still under copyright, so I'm staying close to Rumi's own lines here. Both share the core picture. You're the house, and the moods are guests. A guest comes, stays a while, and leaves. A guest isn't the owner. That changes how you meet a hard morning. Not: I am anxious. But: anxiety is visiting. Offer it a chair, and see what it came to say. It will not stay forever. No guest does. Your line: a guest, not the owner.
screen: `EVERY THOUGHT, AN HONORED GUEST.` · `SORROW SWEEPS THE HOUSE CLEAN.` · `YELLOW LEAVES, THEN GREEN.` · then, large: `A GUEST, NOT THE OWNER.`

segments.voice: Ask: who's visiting right now? Maybe tiredness, maybe hope, maybe a little worry; give it a simple name and greet it inside, the way you'd greet someone at the door: oh, hello, worry, come in. Let it sit with you, and notice it isn't you; it's only staying for a while.
Guest. Rumi says every thought and mood comes into the heart like a guest, and even sorrow may be clearing room for joy. Today's word.
Your line: a guest, not the owner. You're the house. That's day two hundred fourteen.

215.title: Ayaz's sheepskin
215.hook: the king's favorite visits a locked room every day to look at his old sheepskin and shoes (Masnavi 5.1857ff)
215.howItsDone: In Persian poetry Ayaz is a model of loyal, humble love, and readers of Rumi take his sandals and sheepskin as a picture of remembering one's origins with gratitude.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the guest house: every mood a visitor, and you the house. Your line was a guest, not the owner.

Some people keep their first paycheck stub in a drawer. Or the name tag from the diner where they waited tables at sixteen. Or a photo of the tiny apartment with the mattress on the floor. They've done well since. Once in a while they take it out and look at it. Not to feel bad. To remember. This week is called guests, and today's story is about a man who kept a secret room. Every day he went in alone and locked the door. The courtiers were sure he was hiding treasure.
screen: `THE FIRST PAYCHECK STUB.` → `A SECRET ROOM, LOCKED EVERY DAY.` → `AYAZ'S SHEEPSKIN.`

segments.voice: Ayaz turns up in more than one of Rumi's stories. He was the beloved servant of Sultan Mahmud of Ghazni, a real king remembered in Persian history and poetry. Ayaz came to court with nothing and became the king's trusted companion. In Book Five of the Masnavi, Rumi says Ayaz had a little room where he'd hung his old rawhide sandals and his sheepskin jacket, the clothes from his poor days. Every day he'd go in alone, look at them, and say to himself something like: this is where you came from. Don't get proud. The courtiers noticed. A locked room, visited every day, in secret. They whispered to the king: he's hiding gold in there, stolen treasure. The king trusted Ayaz, but he let them look. At midnight they broke in with torches, eager to catch him. And they found a pair of old sandals and a worn sheepskin. That's all. They couldn't believe it. They dug up the floor. They drilled holes in the walls. Nothing. They came back to the king pale and ashamed. There are two ways to hear it. The courtiers are the suspicious mind that assumes everyone is hiding something. And Ayaz, as Rumi reads him, is the soul that remembers its humble origin, not in shame but in gratitude. Remembering the old shoes made the fine robes less dangerous. Your line: the old shoes.

segments.voice: Let an old picture of your life come to mind: a first home, a first job, a hard year, the people who got you through it. Look at it the way Ayaz looked at his sandals, not with shame, not with pride, just: this is where I started. Let some gratitude come if it wants to.
Ayaz's sheepskin. The king's favorite visits his old sandals and sheepskin every day, and the courtiers who break in to find treasure find only those. Today's word.
Your line: the old shoes. The courtiers looked for gold; Ayaz kept sandals. Day two hundred fifteen, done.

216.title: Be one
216.hook: no more arguing about what a good person is; be one (Meditations 10.16)
216.carry: show it by what it produces
216.howItsDone: For the Stoics philosophy was a way of life, and readers of Marcus often use this line to turn from reading and discussion to one concrete good act.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ayaz and his old sandals, and the courtiers who dug and found nothing. Your line was the old shoes.

You can spend a whole evening talking about exercise. Which plan is best, which app, which shoes, what the latest study says. At the end of the evening, you've walked about forty steps, from the couch to the fridge. Planning to be good can feel almost as nice as being good, and it's much less work. For weeks now, Marcus has been thinking hard about how to live. In Book Ten, he seems to catch himself doing just that, and he writes himself one short, blunt sentence.
screen: `AN EVENING ABOUT EXERCISE.` → `FORTY STEPS TO THE FRIDGE.` → `BE ONE.`

segments.voice: Book Ten, section sixteen. In George Long's translation: "No longer talk at all about the kind of man that a good man ought to be, but be such." Stop talking about what a good person is. Be one. You might hear this as a strange thing for Marcus to write; the Meditations is full of thinking about how to be good. But that's the point. It doesn't read like a book written to be admired. It reads like a notebook of reminders, from a man trying to act better the next morning. For the Stoics, philosophy wasn't a topic. It was a way of life. Epictetus, whose sayings Marcus read, made the same point in his Handbook. Don't explain your principles at dinner; eat as a person should. Sheep don't bring their grass to the shepherd to show how much they've eaten. They digest it, and it comes out as wool and milk. Show your principles by what they produce. There's relief in this, too. You don't have to settle every question first, or finish the book, or pass the test, or become an expert in goodness. Right now, there's one kind thing within reach. Do that. Marcus has been saying pieces of this all along: the vine that gives its grapes, stay simple, dig within. Today he just drops the explanation. Your line: show it by what it produces.
screen: `NO LONGER TALK ABOUT IT.` · `A NOTEBOOK, NOT A MONUMENT.` · `SHEEP DON'T SHOW THEIR GRASS.` · then, large: `BE ONE.`

segments.voice: Let the questions about what's right go quiet, and let one simple good act come to mind, something you could do in the next hour: a dish, a message, a kind word, a bit of patience. Don't plan a speech about it. Just see yourself doing it, and rest there.
Be one. Marcus told himself to stop talking about what a good person ought to be, and simply be one. Today's word.
Your line: show it by what it produces. Wool and milk, not grass. See you tomorrow.

217.title: Like leaves
217.hook: Marcus recalls Homer: the generations of people are like leaves in the wind (Meditations 10.34)
217.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus often use short lines like this one, from poets and philosophers, as reminders of how briefly things last, to loosen the grip of praise, blame and fear.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Marcus told himself to stop talking about the good person and be one. Your line was show it by what it produces.

Walk down any street in autumn. The leaves come down in the wind, a few at a time, then all at once. You kick through them. By next spring the same trees will be full again, and none of the new leaves will know about the old ones. Now think about the people who were famous when your grandparents were young. The names everyone knew. How many could you name? Marcus kept a few lines from one of the oldest poems in Greek, and he turned to them to remember something about fame, and loss, and time.
screen: `AUTUMN, AND THEN SPRING.` → `THE NAMES EVERYONE KNEW.` → `LIKE LEAVES.`

segments.voice: The lines come from Homer's Iliad. In the middle of the war at Troy, two warriors meet on the battlefield, and one asks the other who he is. The other answers, more or less: why ask about my family? The generations of people are like leaves. The wind scatters some on the ground, and the forest, when spring comes, grows others. So it is with people: one generation grows, another passes away. In Book Ten, Marcus says that for someone who has taken in the truth, even a short, familiar line like this is enough to free them from grief and fear. Then he applies it, one by one. Your children are leaves. The people who cheer you, and the ones who curse you or sneer behind your back, leaves. The people who will carry your name and reputation after you're gone, leaves too. All come in spring, the wind brings them down, and the forest grows others in their place. That's heavy to hear. Marcus had buried several of his own children. He isn't saying they didn't matter. He's saying how to hold what matters: with open hands. Leaves aren't worthless because they fall. All summer they feed the tree. Each one is beautiful in its season. It just doesn't last forever, and it was never meant to. Praise, insult, even fame after death, all leaves. What's left is how you live this season. Your line: hold it with open hands.
screen: `A LINE FROM HOMER'S ILIAD.` · `THE WIND SCATTERS, THE FOREST GROWS.` · `PRAISE, INSULT, FAME: ALL LEAVES.` · then, large: `LIKE LEAVES.`

segments.voice: If you can, look out a window or step outside and find leaves, grass, or even a plant on a shelf; if you can't, picture a tree in the wind. Watch it move: some leaves hold, some fall, and nothing is wrong. Let your breath move with it.
Like leaves. Marcus recalls Homer: people come and go like leaves in the wind, and the forest grows new ones in the spring. Today's word.
Your line: hold it with open hands. Every leaf still feeds the tree in its season. That's day two hundred seventeen.

original.note: Greek: leaves. from Homer's line comparing the generations of people to leaves.

trapdoor: what you thought: life is short, so nothing matters.
what it means: people, praise and fame come and go like leaves, so hold them with open hands.
what a scholar hears: Iliad 6.146, Glaucus to Diomedes, one of the most quoted lines in Greek poetry, which Marcus adapts to children, critics and posthumous fame.
guess: people and fame come and go, so hold them loosely
people bend with life's winds but never break
fame after death makes a life last forever
recall: a former slave who became a Stoic teacher
a whole too big for any one hand to touch
